add_subtopics.title: Bits, bytes and how data is represented
add_subtopics.body:
Inside a computer everything is stored as bits. A bit is a single 0 or 1, like a switch that is off or on. Counting with only 0 and 1 is called binary: 1, 10, 11, 100 in binary mean 1, 2, 3, 4.

Bits are grouped in eights. Eight bits make one byte, and one byte can hold 256 different values, 0 to 255. Every file on your disk and every value in RAM is a long row of bytes.

What the bytes mean depends on an agreed rule. Text is bytes chosen by an encoding such as UTF-8, where the letter A is the byte 65 and an accented letter like é needs two bytes. Whole numbers are stored in a fixed number of bytes, often 4 or 8. Decimal numbers use a binary format that cannot hold 0.1 exactly, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. An image is bytes describing the colour of each dot, and a PNG file always starts with the same 8 bytes. The dataformats topic covers encodings and number precision in depth.

Sizes are counted in two ways, and this confuses everyone once. Disk makers and network speeds use powers of 1,000: 1 KB = 1,000 bytes, 1 MB = 1,000,000, 1 GB = 1,000,000,000. Operating systems and memory often use powers of 1,024: 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1,024 KiB, 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes, but many tools still print the label GB. That is why a new "512 GB" disk shows about 476 GB free on your laptop: nothing is missing, it is the same bytes divided by a bigger number.
add_subtopics.example: A customer at Fernhollow Surveys complains that their new 512 GB laptop "only has 476 GB" and that a 4-character name, Café, uses 5 bytes in their database. Both have simple answers. 512,000,000,000 bytes divided by 1,073,741,824 is about 476.8, so Windows is showing GiB with a GB label. And in UTF-8 the letters C, a and f take one byte each while é takes two, so the name really is 5 bytes. The code shows both calculations and how the same idea covers numbers and images.
add_subtopics.code:
# Everything a computer stores is bytes: small whole numbers from 0 to 255.
n = 77
print(bin(n), "=", n)                  # 0b1001101 = 77  (bits behind the number)
print(2 ** 8, "values fit in one byte")   # 256 values fit in one byte

# Text is bytes: each character is stored as one or more byte values
word = "Café"
data = word.encode("utf-8")
print(list(data))                      # [67, 97, 102, 195, 169]
print(len(word), "characters,", len(data), "bytes")   # 4 characters, 5 bytes

# Numbers are bytes too: a whole number stored in 4 bytes
print(list((1000).to_bytes(4, "little")))   # [232, 3, 0, 0]

# An image is bytes: every PNG file starts with the same 8 bytes
png_start = bytes([137, 80, 78, 71, 13, 10, 26, 10])
print(png_start[1:4])                  # b'PNG'

# Why a "512 GB" disk shows about 476 GB
disk_bytes = 512 * 1000 ** 3           # makers count 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes
print(round(disk_bytes / 1024 ** 3, 1), "GiB")   # 476.8 GiB, which many tools label "GB"

replace_subtopics.title: The three core parts: CPU, RAM, storage
replace_subtopics.body:
Every computer has a CPU, memory and storage. The CPU does the work: adding numbers, comparing values, moving data around. It is very fast but only holds a tiny amount of data at once.

RAM is where running programs keep their data. It is fast but temporary. When a program ends, or the computer turns off, what was in RAM is gone.

Storage is slower but permanent. Your photos, documents and .py files live here. A laptop might have 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, which is why you can store far more than you can work on at the same moment.

Modern CPUs contain several cores, and each core can run its own stream of instructions. A laptop with 8 cores can truly run 8 processes at the same moment, which is how a slow data job can be split across cores to finish sooner. Python has a rule inside the standard interpreter, the GIL, that lets only one thread run Python code at a time within one process, so to use every core for heavy Python work you start several processes. The asyncpy topic returns to this with ProcessPoolExecutor.

A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a second kind of processor with thousands of small, simple cores. It was built for drawing graphics, but the same trick, doing the same multiplication on huge grids of numbers at once, is exactly what neural networks need. A GPU has its own separate memory called VRAM, for example 24 GB or 80 GB, and a model's weights must fit in VRAM to run quickly. That is why serving or training an LLM needs GPUs with a lot of VRAM, and why running out of VRAM is a common error when a customer tries a bigger open model on their own hardware.
replace_subtopics.example: A small bakery keeps five years of sales in a 2 GB file on its laptop. The laptop has 8 GB of RAM, so a program can load the whole file into memory and add it up. If the file grew to 20 GB, it would still fit on the 512 GB disk, but loading it all into RAM at once would fail. The program would need to read it a piece at a time. The same bakery later wants to rebuild a sales forecast every night. Its old laptop has 4 cores, so the FDE splits the work by shop into 4 processes and the job finishes in about a quarter of the time. For a question-answering assistant, the team compares a cloud LLM API with a model on their own server: the model's weights need about 16 GB, so the server needs a GPU with more than 16 GB of VRAM, not just more ordinary RAM.
replace_subtopics.code:
import os, shutil
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def slow_square(n):
    total = 0
    for _ in range(2_000_000):          # busy work that keeps one core occupied
        total += 1
    return n * n

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # How many CPU cores does this machine have?
    print("CPU cores:", os.cpu_count())

    # How big is the disk, and how much is free? (values are in bytes)
    usage = shutil.disk_usage("/")      # on Windows try "C:\\"
    gib = 1024 ** 3                     # 1 GiB; many OS tools label this "GB"
    print("Disk total GiB:", round(usage.total / gib))
    print("Disk free GiB:", round(usage.free / gib))
    # Disk makers use 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes, so a "512 GB" disk shows about 476 here.

    # Several cores let several processes run at the same moment
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:  # one worker process per core by default
        print(list(pool.map(slow_square, [1, 2, 3, 4])))   # [1, 4, 9, 16]

# Is there an NVIDIA GPU, and how much VRAM does it have? (in a terminal)
#   $ nvidia-smi
#   It lists each GPU, its memory (for example 24576MiB = 24 GiB) and what is using it.
#   "command not found" usually means there is no NVIDIA GPU or no driver installed.

replace_subtopics.title: The operating system
replace_subtopics.body:
The operating system (OS) is the first big program that starts when you switch on a computer. Windows, macOS and Linux are the common ones. Most servers that businesses run in data centres or the cloud use Linux.

The OS starts and stops programs, gives each one its own slice of RAM, lets them read and write files, and passes keyboard input and screen output back and forth. Programs ask the OS for these things instead of touching the hardware directly.

Because each OS does some things differently, such as how file paths are written, a program can behave slightly differently on each one.

Two ideas build on the OS and appear constantly in deployment work. A virtual machine (VM) is a whole pretend computer running as a program on a real one: it gets its own slice of CPU, RAM and disk, and runs its own full operating system. Cloud servers you rent are almost always VMs. A container, such as one run by Docker, is lighter: it shares the host's operating system kernel but gives a program its own private files, packages and settings, so it starts in a second and behaves the same on every machine. Both are "a computer inside a computer", and the deploy and cloud topics use them heavily.
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital's reporting script was written on a Windows laptop and later copied to a Linux server. It failed because it looked for a file at C:\reports\beds.csv, a Windows path that does not exist on Linux. Printing the OS name at the start of the script, as below, is a quick way to see which system you are on. The hospital later packages the script in a container that carries its own Linux files and Python, so it runs the same on the analyst's laptop and on the server.
replace_subtopics.code:
import platform, os

print("Operating system:", platform.system())   # Windows, Darwin (macOS) or Linux
print("OS version:", platform.release())
print("This process id:", os.getpid())           # the OS gives every running program a number
print("Current folder:", os.getcwd())

# A container is its own small Linux, even on a Mac or Windows laptop:
#   $ docker run --rm python:3.12-slim python -c "import platform; print(platform.system())"
#   Linux

replace_subtopics.title: Interpreted Python versus compiled languages
replace_subtopics.body:
The CPU only understands machine code, which is binary instructions specific to that type of chip. Humans write in higher-level languages, so something has to translate.

In a compiled language such as C, C++, Go or Rust, a program called a compiler translates the whole source file ahead of time into a separate executable file. You then run that file directly, and the source is not needed to run it.

Python is usually called interpreted. The standard interpreter, CPython, translates your code into bytecode and runs that bytecode each time you start the program. You skip the build step and can try changes instantly, but the machine running your code must have Python installed, and pure Python loops run slower than compiled code. Libraries such as pandas get speed by doing heavy work in compiled code underneath.

Machine code is specific to a CPU architecture, the family of chip it was built for. Most servers and older PCs use x86_64 (also called amd64). Apple Silicon Macs and cloud chips such as AWS Graviton use ARM64 (also called aarch64). A compiled program or a Docker image built for one will not run on the other: Linux refuses with the message exec format error. This bites FDEs who build an image on an Apple Silicon Mac and deploy it to an x86_64 customer server. Check the architecture with uname -m in a terminal or platform.machine() in Python, and build for the target with docker build --platform linux/amd64. Pure Python files are fine on both, but packages with compiled parts need the right version for the chip, which pip normally picks for you.
replace_subtopics.example: A logistics company has a route-planning tool written in Go and a data-cleaning script written in Python. To ship the Go tool, they compile it once into a single file called routeplan and copy that file to servers. To ship the Python script, they copy clean.py and make sure each server has Python and the right packages installed. Later the logistics team builds the routeplan Docker image on a new Apple Silicon Mac. On the x86_64 server it stops at once with exec format error. uname -m prints arm64 on the Mac and x86_64 on the server, and rebuilding with --platform linux/amd64 fixes it.

add_glossary: Bit
The smallest unit of data, a single 0 or 1.
Byte
A group of 8 bits that can hold one of 256 values; the basic unit of file and memory size.
GiB versus GB
1 GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes (powers of 1,024); 1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes (powers of 1,000).
CPU core
One independent worker inside a CPU; several cores run several processes at the same moment.
GPU and VRAM
A processor with thousands of small cores for maths on large grids of numbers, with its own memory (VRAM) that must hold a model's weights.
CPU architecture
The chip family machine code is built for, such as x86_64 or ARM64.
Virtual machine
A complete simulated computer, with its own operating system, running on real hardware.
Container
A lightweight package that shares the host's OS kernel but carries its own files and packages, such as a Docker container.

Run uname -m (or print platform.machine() in Python) and os.cpu_count() on your computer. Write one sentence saying whether a Docker image built on your machine would run unchanged on an x86_64 server.

add_subtopics.title: Working with files from the shell
add_subtopics.body:
Most FDE work in a terminal is handling files: customer exports, logs and scripts. A small set of commands covers it.

touch name makes an empty file. cat name prints a whole file, which is fine for short files. head -n 5 shows the first 5 lines and tail -n 5 the last 5, perfect for peeking at a 2 GB CSV without opening it. tail -f follows a log as new lines arrive. less lets you scroll a big file with the arrow keys; press q to quit.

cp copies, mv moves or renames, and rm deletes. rm -r deletes a folder and everything inside it. Be careful: the shell has no recycle bin, so a deleted file is gone for good. Read the command twice before pressing Enter, especially with rm -r.

A wildcard lets one command match many files. *.csv means every name ending in .csv, so cp *.csv backup/ copies them all. The shell expands the pattern before running the command.

Spaces split arguments. A folder called client files looks like two names, client and files, so wrap it in quotes: "client files". Pressing Tab adds the quoting or backslashes for you.

On Windows Command Prompt the names differ: type instead of cat, copy, move, del and rmdir /s. PowerShell accepts cat, cp, mv, rm and ls as aliases, so the Mac and Linux commands mostly work there too.
add_subtopics.example: A customer at Brightwell Logistics sends twelve monthly CSV files. The FDE uses head -n 2 on one file to see the column names, ls *.csv to confirm all twelve arrived, and cp *.csv into a folder called "raw exports" with quotes because of the space. When she deletes an old test file with rm, she knows it is not in any bin, so she checks the name with ls first.
add_subtopics.code:
touch notes.txt                 # make an empty file (PowerShell: New-Item notes.txt)
cat sales_jan.csv               # print a whole file (Windows cmd: type)
head -n 2 sales_jan.csv         # first 2 lines
# order_id,amount
# 1001,25.00
tail -n 1 sales_jan.csv         # last line
# 1003,12.75
less sales_jan.csv              # scroll a big file; press q to quit

cp sales_jan.csv sales_feb.csv  # copy          (cmd: copy)
mv notes.txt readme.txt         # rename/move   (cmd: move)
ls *.csv                        # wildcard: every file ending in .csv
# sales_feb.csv
# sales_jan.csv
rm sales_feb.csv                # delete a file (cmd: del). No recycle bin!
rm -r old_exports               # delete a folder and everything inside it

mkdir "client files"            # quotes keep a name with a space together
cp sales_jan.csv "client files/"
ls client files                 # WRONG: the shell sees two names, client and files

add_subtopics.title: Output, redirection and exit codes
add_subtopics.body:
Every command has two output streams. stdout (standard output) carries normal results. stderr (standard error) carries error messages. Both appear on screen, but you can send them to different places.

> sends stdout into a file and overwrites whatever was there. >> appends to the end instead, which is what you want for a log. 2> redirects only stderr, and 2>&1 means "send stderr to wherever stdout is going", so command > run.log 2>&1 captures everything in one file. That is exactly the tail of a typical cron line. < does the reverse and feeds a file in as input.

A pipe, written |, sends one command's output straight into the next command. cat file | grep 1002 shows only lines containing 1002. Pipes let small tools combine into powerful one-liners.

Every command also finishes with an exit code, a number the shell keeps in $? (PowerShell: $LASTEXITCODE). 0 means success and anything else means something failed. Scripts, cron and CI systems rely on this number to decide whether a step worked. Your own Python script can set it with sys.exit(1).

You can chain commands on the exit code. a && b runs b only if a succeeded, so a failed step stops the chain. a || b runs b only if a failed, which is handy for a fallback message.
add_subtopics.example: A nightly job at Harlow Dental runs python export.py > export.log 2>&1 && python upload.py. One night the database is down, export.py prints a traceback to stderr and exits with code 1. Because of 2>&1 the traceback is in export.log, and because of && the upload never runs with a half-finished file. The FDE reads the log the next morning and sees exactly what failed.
add_subtopics.code:
ls sales_jan.csv > out.txt       # stdout goes into out.txt (overwrites it)
echo first > log.txt             # log.txt now holds: first
echo second >> log.txt           # >> appends; log.txt holds: first, second
cat log.txt
# first
# second

ls nothere                       # an error goes to stderr
# ls: cannot access 'nothere': No such file or directory
echo $?                          # exit code of the last command
# 2                                (0 means success; PowerShell: $LASTEXITCODE)
ls nothere > err.txt 2>&1        # send stdout AND stderr into the file

cat sales_jan.csv | grep 1002    # a pipe feeds one command's output to the next
# 1002,40.50
wc -l < sales_jan.csv            # < reads a file as input: counts the lines
# 4

mkdir backup && cp sales_jan.csv backup/ && echo "backup done"   # && runs next only on success
# backup done
ls nothere 2>/dev/null || echo "no such file"                    # || runs only on failure
# no such file

rows: Send stdout to a file, overwriting it
Send stderr to the same place as stdout
Pipe stdout into the next command
Exit code of the last command (0 = success)
Run the next command only on success / only on failure

replace_subtopics.title: What a terminal and shell are
replace_subtopics.body:
When you open Terminal on a Mac, a terminal app on Linux, or PowerShell on Windows, you see a prompt: a short line of text ending in something like $ or >. The prompt means the shell is waiting for you.

You type a command, which is usually a program name followed by extra words called arguments, then press Enter. The shell runs it and prints any output. Then it shows the prompt again.

Commands are case sensitive on Mac and Linux. Typing Ls instead of ls will fail there.

Many commands accept options, also called flags, that change what they do. A short flag is a dash and a letter, such as ls -l for a long listing with sizes and dates. A long flag uses two dashes, such as --help, which prints a summary of every option. On Mac and Linux, man ls opens the full manual page; press q to leave it.

A few keys save a lot of time. Ctrl+C stops a command that is running too long or is stuck. The Up arrow brings back your previous commands, and Ctrl+R searches your history as you type. clear wipes the screen (cls in Command Prompt).

If you see command not found (Windows: is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet), the shell looked in every folder listed in PATH and did not find the program. Either it is not installed or its folder is not in PATH. which python3 on Mac and Linux, or where python on Windows, shows which file will run.
replace_subtopics.example: A new analyst at an insurance company opens a terminal for the first time and types three commands. whoami prints her username, jsmith. echo hello prints hello back. date prints today's date and time. Each command runs, prints one line, and returns her to the prompt. Later she runs ls -l to see file sizes, and python3 --help to see Python's options. A script she starts loops forever, so she presses Ctrl+C to stop it. When she types jupyter and gets command not found, which jupyter prints nothing, which tells her it is not installed in the current environment.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Lines starting with # are comments; the shell ignores them.
# Type each command after the prompt and press Enter.
whoami            # prints your username
echo hello        # prints the word hello
date              # prints the current date and time (Mac/Linux)
Get-Date          # the PowerShell version of date on Windows

ls -l             # a flag: long listing with sizes and dates
ls --help         # list every option (Mac: man ls)
man ls            # full manual; press q to quit
which python3     # which program runs (Windows: where python)
# /usr/bin/python3
clear             # clear the screen (cmd: cls)
# Ctrl+C stops a running command, Up arrow repeats, Ctrl+R searches history

replace_subtopics.title: Folders, paths and where you are
replace_subtopics.body:
Files live in folders, and folders sit inside other folders like a tree. A path is the address of a file or folder.

An absolute path starts from the very top. On Mac and Linux the top is written /, and folders are separated by forward slashes: /Users/asha/projects/report.csv. On Windows each drive has its own top, such as C:\, and folders are separated by backslashes: C:\Users\asha\projects\report.csv.

The shell is always standing in one folder called the current working directory. A relative path starts from there. If you are in /Users/asha, the relative path projects/report.csv points to the same file. Two dots, .., mean the folder one level up, and a single dot means the current folder. The symbol ~ is a shortcut for your home folder on Mac and Linux, and works in PowerShell too.

Windows backslashes cause a classic bug inside Python code. In a normal Python string a backslash starts an escape: \n means newline and \t means tab. So "C:\new\data.csv" silently turns \n into a line break. Put an r in front to make a raw string, r"C:\new\data.csv", or use forward slashes, which Windows Python also accepts. Better still, use pathlib, which joins folder names with the right separator on every system.
replace_subtopics.example:
A retail analyst is in /Users/asha. The weekly file is at /Users/asha/projects/sales/week1.csv. From /Users/asha she can refer to it as projects/sales/week1.csv. If she moves into /Users/asha/projects/sales, she can just type week1.csv. If she moves into a sibling folder /Users/asha/projects/stock, the same file is ../sales/week1.csv. Her Windows colleague writes open("C:
ew\data.csv") and gets a confusing error, because Python read 
 as a newline. Changing it to r"C:
ew\data.csv" fixes it.

Mac / Linux                          Windows
-----------                          -------
/                                    C:\
/Users/asha                          C:\Users\asha
/Users/asha/projects/sales           C:\Users\asha\projects\sales

Absolute: /Users/asha/projects/sales/week1.csv
Relative from /Users/asha:        projects/sales/week1.csv
Relative from .../projects/stock: ../sales/week1.csv
.   = this folder
..  = one folder up
~   = your home folder

# In Python:
from pathlib import Path
print("C:\new\data.csv")     # \n became a newline!
# C:
# ew\data.csv
print(r"C:\new\data.csv")    # raw string keeps the backslashes
# C:\new\data.csv
print(Path("reports") / "2026" / "sales.csv")   # right separator on any OS
# reports/2026/sales.csv   (Windows prints reports\2026\sales.csv)

replace_subtopics.title: pip and virtual environments
replace_subtopics.body:
A package (or library) is ready-made code someone else wrote, such as requests for talking to websites or pandas for tables. pip is the tool that downloads and installs packages, usually from PyPI, the Python Package Index.

If you install everything into one shared Python, different projects start to clash: one needs pandas 1.5, another needs pandas 2.2. A virtual environment solves this. It is a folder, commonly named .venv, containing its own Python and its own packages for one project.

You create it once, activate it each time you open a new terminal, and then pip installs into it. The prompt usually shows (.venv) when it is active. pip freeze > requirements.txt records the exact versions so someone else can recreate the same setup with pip install -r requirements.txt.

Always check that the venv is really active before installing. which python (Mac and Linux) or where python (Windows) should print a path inside your project's .venv folder. If it shows a system path, pip will install into the wrong Python.

On Windows PowerShell, activation can fail with running scripts is disabled on this system. That is a safety setting, not a broken venv. Run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned once, then activate again with .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1. Windows users who want the same commands as Mac and Linux can install WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which gives a real Linux shell inside Windows.
replace_subtopics.example: An FDE starts work for a grocery chain. In the project folder she creates .venv, activates it, installs requests and pandas, and saves requirements.txt. A colleague clones the project on Windows, creates his own .venv, activates it with the Windows command and runs pip install -r requirements.txt. Both now have identical package versions. Her Windows colleague first sees running scripts is disabled when activating. He runs the Set-ExecutionPolicy line once, activates again, and where python now lists the .venv path first.
replace_subtopics.code:
cd grocery-project
python3 -m venv .venv              # create the virtual environment (once)

source .venv/bin/activate          # Mac/Linux: activate it
# .venv\Scripts\activate           # Windows equivalent

python -m pip install requests pandas   # installs into .venv only
pip freeze > requirements.txt      # record exact versions

pip install -r requirements.txt    # a colleague recreates the same set
deactivate                         # leave the venv when done

which python                       # Mac/Linux: should end in .venv/bin/python
# where python                     # Windows: first line should be ...\.venv\Scripts\python.exe

# PowerShell error: "running scripts is disabled on this system"
# Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned   (run once)
# .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

replace_subtopics.title: Environment variables
replace_subtopics.body:
An environment variable is a named piece of text that the shell passes to every program it starts. PATH is one you already rely on: it lists the folders the shell searches when you type a command such as python.

You can set your own. This is the standard place for settings that change between machines and for secrets like API keys (a password-like string that lets a program use an online service). Keeping them out of the code means you can share the code safely.

A variable set with export or $env: lasts only for that terminal window. Close the window and it is gone, which is often what you want for secrets.

To make a variable permanent on Mac or Linux, add the export line to your shell's startup file: ~/.zshrc for zsh (the Mac default) or ~/.bashrc for bash, then open a new terminal. On Windows, setx NAME value saves it for future windows, or add the line to your PowerShell profile.

For project settings, most Python projects use a .env file instead: a plain text file of NAME=value lines in the project folder. The python-dotenv package (pip install python-dotenv) loads it with load_dotenv(), and os.environ then sees the values. A .env file usually holds secrets, so add .env to .gitignore before your first commit so it never reaches Git.
replace_subtopics.example: A payments startup's script needs a key to call a currency API. Instead of writing the key into convert.py, the FDE sets CURRENCY_KEY in the terminal. The script reads it with os.environ.get. On the customer's server, their admin sets their own key the same way and the code does not change. Later the FDE moves the key into a .env file containing CURRENCY_KEY=test-123, calls load_dotenv() at the top of convert.py, and adds .env to .gitignore so the key is never committed.
replace_subtopics.code:
# In the shell (Mac/Linux):
export CURRENCY_KEY="test-123"
# In PowerShell (Windows):
# $env:CURRENCY_KEY="test-123"
echo $CURRENCY_KEY            # check it is set (PowerShell: echo $env:CURRENCY_KEY)

# convert.py
import os
key = os.environ.get("CURRENCY_KEY")   # None if it was never set
if key is None:
    print("Please set CURRENCY_KEY first")
else:
    print("Using a key that starts with", key[:4])

# Make it permanent (Mac zsh):
# echo 'export CURRENCY_KEY="test-123"' >> ~/.zshrc
# Windows: setx CURRENCY_KEY "test-123"

# .env file in the project folder:
#   CURRENCY_KEY=test-123
# .gitignore:
#   .env

# convert.py with python-dotenv
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()                          # reads .env in the current folder
key = os.environ.get("CURRENCY_KEY")
print("Using a key that starts with", key[:4])
# Using a key that starts with test

add_glossary: Flag
An option added to a command to change what it does, such as -l or --help.
Wildcard
A pattern such as *.csv that the shell expands into every matching file name.
stdout and stderr
The two output streams of a command: normal results and error messages.
Redirection
Sending a command's output to a file with > (overwrite) or >> (append), or reading input with <.
Pipe
The | symbol, which feeds one command's output into the next command.
Exit code
A number a command returns when it finishes; 0 means success.
PATH
The environment variable listing folders the shell searches for commands.
.env file
A text file of NAME=value settings loaded by tools such as python-dotenv; never committed to Git.
Raw string
A Python string written r"..." in which backslashes are kept as plain characters.
WSL
Windows Subsystem for Linux: a real Linux shell running inside Windows.

add_subtopics.title: Working with strings
add_subtopics.body:
A huge share of FDE work is cleaning text: names, emails, product codes, free-text notes. Python strings come with many built-in tools.

Indexing picks one character by position, counting from 0: name[0] is the first character and name[-1] the last. Slicing takes a range: name[0:5] gives characters 0 up to, but not including, 5. len(name) gives the length.

Methods are functions attached to the string, called with a dot. lower() and upper() change case, and title() capitalises each word. strip() removes spaces and line breaks from both ends, which fixes many messy exports. split(",") breaks a string into a list at each comma, and " ".join(list) does the reverse. replace(old, new) swaps text, and startswith and endswith test the ends. The in operator checks whether one string appears inside another: "@" in email. Strings never change in place; each method returns a new string, so you must assign the result.

f-strings accept a format spec after a colon: {x:.2f} shows two decimal places, {n:,} adds thousands separators, and {r:.1%} shows a percentage.

A backslash starts an escape character: \n is a new line, \t a tab, and \\ a real backslash. The pandas .str methods you meet later are these same string methods applied to a whole column.
add_subtopics.example: A customer record from Larkspur Travel arrives as "  Maria GARCIA , maria@Example.com  ". split(",") separates name and email, strip() removes the stray spaces, title() fixes the name's capitals and lower() makes the email comparable. A report line then shows revenue of 1234567.891 as 1,234,567.89 with {total:,.2f}.
add_subtopics.code:
raw = "  Maria GARCIA , maria@Example.com  "
name, email = raw.split(",")          # split on the comma -> two strings
name = name.strip().title()           # remove outer spaces, capitalise words
email = email.strip().lower()
print(name, "|", email)               # Maria Garcia | maria@example.com
print(len(name), name[0], name[-1], name[0:5])   # 12 M a Maria

print(email.endswith(".com"), "@" in email)       # True True
print(email.replace("example.com", "example.org"))  # maria@example.org
print(" ".join(["Hello", name]))      # Hello Maria Garcia

total, orders = 1234567.891, 1520
print(f"Revenue: {total:,.2f}  Orders: {orders:,}  Share: {0.4567:.1%}")
# Revenue: 1,234,567.89  Orders: 1,520  Share: 45.7%
print("Name:\tMaria\nCity:\tLagos")   # \t is a tab, \n starts a new line
# Name:   Maria
# City:   Lagos
print("Folder: C:\\data")             # Folder: C:\data   (\\ prints one backslash)

replace_subtopics.title: Variables and the four basic types
replace_subtopics.body:
A variable is a name that points to a value. You create one with a single equals sign: price = 4. From then on, price means 4 until you change it. Names can use letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit.

Every value has a type that decides what you can do with it. int is a whole number such as 42. float is a number with a decimal point such as 3.99. str (string) is text in quotes such as "Lagos". bool is either True or False.

The type matters. 2 + 3 gives 5, but "2" + "3" gives "23" because adding strings joins them. type(x) tells you what type a value has.

One more special value is None, which means "no value yet" or "nothing here". Test for it with x is None, not x == None.

Every value also counts as true or false inside an if. This is called truthiness. 0, 0.0, an empty string "", an empty list [] and None all count as False; almost everything else counts as True. So if name: means "if name is not empty".

Three more arithmetic operators are worth knowing. // is floor division, which drops the remainder: 17 // 5 is 3. % gives the remainder: 17 % 5 is 2, handy for "every 5th row". ** is power: 2 ** 10 is 1024.

Floats are stored in binary and cannot hold most decimals exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004 and 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. round() also surprises people: round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4, because Python rounds exact halves to the nearest even number (banker's rounding). round(2.675, 2) gives 2.67 because 2.675 is really stored as slightly less. For money, use the Decimal type, covered in the dataformats topic.
replace_subtopics.example: A coffee shop records one order. cups is an int, 2. price is a float, 3.50. customer is a str, "Maria". paid is a bool, False. The total is cups times price, 7.0. Joining customer with " owes " and the total needs str(total), because you cannot add a string and a float directly. The shop also stores discount = None until a manager sets one, and checks it with is None. Splitting 17 cups into boxes of 5 gives 17 // 5 = 3 full boxes and 17 % 5 = 2 left over.
replace_subtopics.code:
cups = 2              # int
price = 3.50          # float
customer = "Maria"    # str
paid = False          # bool

total = cups * price  # 7.0
print(type(cups), type(price), type(customer), type(paid))
print(customer + " owes " + str(total))   # Maria owes 7.0
print("2" + "3")      # 23  (joining text)
print(2 + 3)          # 5   (adding numbers)

discount = None                  # None means "no value yet"
if discount is None:             # use 'is None', not '== None'
    print("No discount set")     # No discount set

for value in [0, "", [], None, 5, "hi"]:
    print(repr(value), bool(value))
# 0 False / '' False / [] False / None False / 5 True / 'hi' True

print(17 // 5, 17 % 5, 2 ** 10)  # 3 2 1024  (floor division, remainder, power)
print(0.1 + 0.2, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)       # 0.30000000000000004 False
print(round(2.5), round(3.5), round(2.675, 2))   # 2 4 2.67

replace_subtopics.title: Functions: parameters and return values
replace_subtopics.body:
A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. You define one with def, a name, parameters in brackets and a colon. Parameters are the named inputs the function expects.

When you call the function, you pass arguments, the actual values for those parameters. The body runs, and return sends a result back to the caller, ending the function at that point. A function with no return gives back the special value None.

Good functions do one clear job and have a name that says what it is. They save you copying the same lines in several places, and they are easy to test on their own.

A parameter can have a default value: def price_with_tax(nightly_rate, nights=1) lets callers leave nights out. When calling, you can name arguments, price_with_tax(100, nights=2), which makes the call easier to read and lets you give them in any order.

Variables created inside a function are local: they exist only while it runs, and code outside cannot see them. Variables defined at the top of the file are global and can be read inside functions. Pass values in as parameters rather than relying on globals.

A docstring is a string on the first line of the function body that says what it does; help() prints it. Type hints such as nightly_rate: float and -> float note the expected types. Python does not enforce them, but editors and checkers use them to catch mistakes.

Python also ships with a standard library of ready modules. import math gives you math.ceil and math.sqrt, and from datetime import date imports one name directly. These need no installing. pip install is only for third-party packages such as requests or pandas.
replace_subtopics.example: A hotel adds 12 percent tax to room prices and gives a 10 dollar discount on stays of three nights or more. The function price_with_tax takes nightly_rate and nights. For 100 dollars and 3 nights it computes 300, subtracts 10 to get 290, adds tax and returns 324.8. The same function is then reused for a second booking of 80 dollars for 1 night, which returns 89.6. The hotel function gains a default of one night and a docstring, and the booking code calls it with nights=2 so the meaning is obvious. It also imports math and datetime from the standard library without installing anything.
replace_subtopics.code:
def price_with_tax(nightly_rate, nights):   # two parameters
    subtotal = nightly_rate * nights
    if nights >= 3:
        subtotal = subtotal - 10            # long-stay discount
    return round(subtotal * 1.12, 2)        # send the answer back

booking1 = price_with_tax(100, 3)           # arguments 100 and 3
booking2 = price_with_tax(80, 1)
print(booking1, booking2)                   # 324.8 89.6

import math                       # standard library: comes with Python
from datetime import date         # import one name from a module

TAX_RATE = 0.12                   # global: defined outside any function

def price_with_tax(nightly_rate: float, nights: int = 1) -> float:
    """Return the total price for a stay, including tax."""
    subtotal = nightly_rate * nights             # subtotal is local to this function
    return round(subtotal * (1 + TAX_RATE), 2)

print(price_with_tax(80))                        # 89.6   (nights defaults to 1)
print(price_with_tax(100, nights=2))             # 224.0  (keyword argument)
print(price_with_tax(nights=2, nightly_rate=100))  # 224.0 (order does not matter)
print(math.ceil(7 / 3), date(2026, 3, 1).isoformat())   # 3 2026-03-01
# print(subtotal)  -> NameError: subtotal only exists inside the function
help(price_with_tax)              # prints the signature and the docstring

replace_subtopics.title: Errors and reading a traceback
replace_subtopics.body:
When Python hits a problem it cannot handle, it raises an exception and stops. It prints a traceback, a report of what happened.

Read it from the bottom up. The last line gives the error type and a message, such as ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'thirty'. The line just above shows the code that failed, and above that is the file name and line number. If functions called other functions, each call appears as a pair of lines, oldest at the top.

Common types are SyntaxError (the code breaks Python's grammar), NameError (a name that was never defined, often a typo), TypeError (wrong type for the operation), ValueError (right type, bad value) and ZeroDivisionError. You can catch an expected error with try and except so the program can respond instead of crashing.

You can raise your own errors when a value makes no sense: raise ValueError("quantity cannot be negative"). This stops bad data early with a clear message.

Catch specific exceptions, such as except ValueError, rather than a bare except:. A bare except also hides typos and even Ctrl+C, so real bugs go unnoticed. Write except ValueError as e: and print(e) to show the error's message. A finally block runs whether or not an error happened, which is where clean-up such as closing a file goes.
replace_subtopics.example: A pharmacy's stock script asks for a quantity. A user types thirty. The traceback's last line says ValueError and quotes 'thirty', and the line above points to line 3 of stock.py. The fix wraps the conversion in try/except and asks the user to type digits. Later the stock script raises its own ValueError for a negative quantity, catches it with except ValueError as e, and prints the message, while finally logs every input it checked.
replace_subtopics.code:
# What the crash looks like:
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "/home/asha/stock.py", line 3, in <module>
#     qty = int(input("Quantity: "))
# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'thirty'

# The fix: expect the error and handle it
while True:
    try:
        qty = int(input("Quantity: "))
        break                                 # leave the loop on success
    except ValueError:
        print("Please type a whole number, like 30")
print("Recorded", qty, "boxes")

def set_quantity(qty):
    if qty < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"quantity cannot be negative, got {qty}")
    return qty

for text in ["30", "thirty", "-5"]:
    try:
        qty = set_quantity(int(text))
        print("Recorded", qty)
    except ValueError as e:              # catch only the error you expect
        print("Rejected:", e)
    finally:
        print("checked", repr(text))     # runs whether or not there was an error
# Recorded 30
# checked '30'
# Rejected: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'thirty'
# checked 'thirty'
# Rejected: quantity cannot be negative, got -5
# checked '-5'

add_glossary: None
Python's value for "nothing here"; test it with is None.
Truthiness
How a value behaves in an if: 0, empty strings, empty lists and None count as False.
Floor division
The // operator, which divides and drops the remainder.
Modulo
The % operator, which gives the remainder of a division.
Slice
A range of positions taken from a string or list, such as s[0:5].
Default argument
A parameter value used when the caller leaves that argument out.
Local variable
A variable created inside a function that exists only while the function runs.
Docstring
A string at the top of a function that describes what it does.
Type hint
A note such as x: int that says what type a value should be; not enforced at run time.
Standard library
The modules that come with Python, such as math and datetime, needing no install.

add_subtopics.title: Nested data from APIs
add_subtopics.body:
Real data is rarely one flat list or one flat dict. Almost every API response an FDE handles is nested: a dict that holds a list, where each item is another dict, which may hold more dicts and lists.

You reach inside by chaining lookups, reading left to right. data["items"] is the list of orders, data["items"][0] is the first order (a dict), and data["items"][0]["price"] is its price. Print one level at a time when you are unsure of the shape.

Real responses are inconsistent: one order has a city, the next does not. A direct lookup on a missing key raises KeyError and stops the script. Chaining .get with a sensible default avoids that: item.get("customer", {}).get("city", "unknown"). The empty dict {} as the first default means the second .get still works when the whole customer block is missing.

The two common shapes are a list of dicts (one dict per record, the usual API shape) and a dict of lists (a key such as a city pointing to many values). To load API data into a spreadsheet or a DataFrame you flatten it into rows: loop over the list and build one flat dict per record, or call pd.json_normalize, which turns nested keys into columns such as customer.name. Lists inside a record, such as tags, need a decision: join them into one string or give each value its own row.
add_subtopics.example: An orders API used by Tidewater Outfitters returns a page with an items list. The FDE reads the first price with data["items"][0]["price"], finds that one customer has no city, and switches to chained .get calls. She flattens each order into a row with id, price, name, city and a comma-joined tags field, and checks the same result with pd.json_normalize before saving the rows to CSV.
add_subtopics.code:
import pandas as pd

# The shape a typical orders API returns (response.json() gives you this)
data = {
    "page": 1,
    "items": [
        {"id": "A-100", "price": 25.0, "customer": {"name": "Lena", "city": "Porto"},
         "tags": ["gift", "express"]},
        {"id": "A-101", "price": 40.5, "customer": {"name": "Omar"}, "tags": []},
    ],
}

print(data["items"][0]["price"])                   # 25.0
print(data["items"][0]["customer"]["city"])        # Porto
# data["items"][1]["customer"]["city"]  -> KeyError: 'city'
print(data["items"][1].get("customer", {}).get("city", "unknown"))   # unknown

rows = []                                          # flatten by hand: one dict per row
for item in data.get("items", []):
    cust = item.get("customer", {})
    rows.append({"id": item["id"], "price": item["price"],
                 "name": cust.get("name"), "city": cust.get("city"),
                 "tags": ",".join(item.get("tags", []))})
print(rows[1])
# {'id': 'A-101', 'price': 40.5, 'name': 'Omar', 'city': None, 'tags': ''}

df = pd.json_normalize(data["items"])              # or let pandas flatten it
print(df.columns.tolist())
# ['id', 'price', 'tags', 'customer.name', 'customer.city']

by_city = {"Porto": ["A-100", "A-107"], "Lyon": ["A-101"]}   # a dict of lists
print(len(by_city["Porto"]))                       # 2

replace_subtopics.title: Lists and tuples
replace_subtopics.body:
A list holds items in order inside square brackets: ["tea", "coffee", "juice"]. Each item has a position called an index, counting from 0, so the first item is at index 0. Negative indexes count from the end, so -1 is the last item.

Lists can change. append adds an item at the end, remove deletes one by value, and you can replace an item by assigning to its index. len(list) gives the number of items. A slice such as items[0:2] gives a new list of the items at indexes 0 and 1.

A tuple uses round brackets: (51.5, -0.12). It is ordered like a list but cannot be changed after it is made. Use it for small fixed groups of values, such as a latitude and longitude pair.

To put items in order, sorted(items) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone, while items.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None (so never write x = items.sort()). Both take key=, a function that picks what to sort by: key=lambda r: r["amount"] sorts a list of dicts by amount. A lambda is a tiny unnamed function written on one line. reverse=True sorts from largest to smallest.

enumerate(items) gives the position and the item together, and zip(a, b) walks two lists side by side.

Lists are mutable, and a variable only points at a list. b = a does not copy anything: a and b are two names for one list, so changing b changes a. This is called aliasing. Use a.copy() or list(a) for a new list. If the list holds dicts or other lists, a normal copy still shares those inner items, so use copy.deepcopy for a fully independent copy.
replace_subtopics.example: A bakery tracks today's orders in a list. It starts with three: croissant, bagel, muffin. A fourth order, scone, is appended. The bagel is cancelled and removed. The list now has three items, and the last one is scone. The shop's location is stored as a tuple so no code can change it by accident. Later the bakery sorts its orders by amount, largest first, with sorted and a lambda. A helper that did b = orders and then appended a test order accidentally changed the real list, which orders.copy() fixes.
replace_subtopics.code:
orders = ["croissant", "bagel", "muffin"]
orders.append("scone")        # add to the end
orders.remove("bagel")        # remove by value
print(orders)                 # ['croissant', 'muffin', 'scone']
print(orders[0], orders[-1])  # croissant scone
print(len(orders))            # 3
print(orders[0:2])            # ['croissant', 'muffin']

shop_location = (51.5074, -0.1278)   # a tuple: latitude, longitude
lat, lon = shop_location             # unpack into two variables
# shop_location[0] = 0  would raise TypeError: tuples cannot change

orders = [{"id": 1, "amount": 40}, {"id": 2, "amount": 15}, {"id": 3, "amount": 90}]

biggest = sorted(orders, key=lambda r: r["amount"], reverse=True)   # new list
print([r["id"] for r in biggest])        # [3, 1, 2]
nums = [5, 2, 9]
nums.sort()                              # sorts in place, returns None
print(nums)                              # [2, 5, 9]

for pos, r in enumerate(orders, start=1):
    print(pos, r["id"])                  # 1 1 / 2 2 / 3 3
names = ["tea", "cake"]
prices = [4.5, 12.0]
for n, p in zip(names, prices):
    print(n, p)                          # tea 4.5 / cake 12.0

a = ["croissant", "bagel"]
b = a                    # b is the SAME list, not a copy
b.append("scone")
print(a)                 # ['croissant', 'bagel', 'scone']  a changed too!
c = a.copy()             # a real (shallow) copy
c.append("muffin")
print(len(a), len(c))    # 3 4

import copy
nested = [{"qty": 1}]
shallow = nested.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(nested)
shallow[0]["qty"] = 99   # the inner dict is still shared by a shallow copy
print(nested[0]["qty"], deep[0]["qty"])   # 99 1

replace_subtopics.title: Dicts and sets
replace_subtopics.body:
A dict (dictionary) stores pairs of key and value inside curly braces: {"name": "Ravi", "age": 34}. You look a value up by its key: person["name"]. Keys are usually strings or numbers and must be unique. Assigning to a key adds it or replaces its value.

If you ask for a key that is missing, Python raises KeyError. The get method returns a default instead: person.get("email", "none"). Looping over a dict with .items() gives you each key and value together.

A set holds unique values with no order: {"North", "South"}. Adding a value that is already there does nothing. Sets are the quickest way to remove duplicates or check whether something is present.

The collections module in the standard library has two dict helpers FDEs use constantly. Counter counts things for you: Counter(visits) gives how many times each value appears, and most_common(3) gives the top three. defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time a key is used, so grouping records needs no "is the key there yet?" check.

Sets support maths-style operations that answer business questions directly. a & b is the intersection, the values in both. a | b is the union, the values in either. a - b is the difference, the values in a but not in b, such as customers who bought last month but not this month.
replace_subtopics.example: A clinic keeps one patient's details in a dict with keys name, age and ward. A nurse updates the ward from B to C. Asking for email with get returns the default "not recorded" instead of crashing. Separately, the list of wards visited today, ["A", "C", "A", "B", "C"], becomes the set {"A", "B", "C"}, so the clinic knows three wards were involved. The clinic counts visits per ward with Counter and finds ward A busiest. A retailer groups orders by store with defaultdict(list), and uses last_month - this_month to list customers who did not come back.
replace_subtopics.code:
patient = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 34, "ward": "B"}
patient["ward"] = "C"                       # update a value
print(patient["name"])                      # Ravi
print(patient.get("email", "not recorded")) # safe lookup with a default

for key, value in patient.items():          # loop over pairs
    print(key, "=", value)

visits = ["A", "C", "A", "B", "C"]
wards = set(visits)                         # duplicates disappear
print(len(wards), "wards")                  # 3 wards
print("B" in wards)                         # True

from collections import Counter, defaultdict

visits = ["A", "C", "A", "B", "C", "A"]
counts = Counter(visits)
print(counts)                    # Counter({'A': 3, 'C': 2, 'B': 1})
print(counts.most_common(1))     # [('A', 3)]

orders = [("North", "tea"), ("South", "cake"), ("North", "bun")]
by_store = defaultdict(list)     # missing keys start as an empty list
for store, item in orders:
    by_store[store].append(item)
print(dict(by_store))            # {'North': ['tea', 'bun'], 'South': ['cake']}

last_month = {"ana", "ben", "cai"}
this_month = {"ben", "cai", "dev"}
print(sorted(last_month & this_month))   # both months:    ['ben', 'cai']
print(sorted(last_month | this_month))   # either month:   ['ana', 'ben', 'cai', 'dev']
print(sorted(last_month - this_month))   # lost customers: ['ana']

replace_subtopics.title: Reading and writing files, and JSON
replace_subtopics.body:
open(path, mode) connects your program to a file. Mode "r" reads (the default), "w" writes and replaces any existing contents, and "a" appends to the end. Always use it inside a with block, which closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens.

f.read() returns the whole file as one string. Looping with for line in f gives one line at a time, which is better for large files because it does not load everything into RAM at once. Each line ends with a newline character, which strip() removes.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format that looks almost like Python dicts and lists and is used by most web APIs. The json module converts in both directions: json.dump writes a Python value to a file, json.load reads it back, and json.dumps and json.loads do the same with strings.

Always pass encoding="utf-8" when opening text files. Without it, Python uses the system default, which on many Windows machines is cp1252, so names like Café break or crash. The dataformats topic explains encodings in depth.

pathlib.Path builds file paths that work on every operating system: Path("data") / "jan.csv" uses the right separator. Path("data").glob("*.csv") loops over every CSV in a folder, which is how you process a folder of monthly exports.

json.dumps only understands basic types: dicts, lists, strings, numbers, True, False and None. A datetime or Decimal raises TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable. Either pass default=str so unknown objects are turned into strings, or convert them yourself first, for example with .isoformat() for dates and str() for Decimal amounts.
replace_subtopics.example: A small hotel logs guest check-ins to checkins.txt, one name per line, using append mode so earlier names are kept. At night a script reads the file and counts 3 guests. It saves a summary dict, date and count, to summary.json. The next morning another script loads summary.json and gets the same dict back. Later the hotel stores check-in times as datetime values. json.dumps raises TypeError until the script converts them with isoformat(). It also reads a folder of monthly CSV exports with Path("data").glob("*.csv"), always with encoding="utf-8".
replace_subtopics.code:
import json

with open("checkins.txt", "a") as f:          # "a" adds to the end
    for name in ["Lee", "Okafor", "Silva"]:
        f.write(name + "\n")                   # \n starts a new line

with open("checkins.txt") as f:
    names = [line.strip() for line in f]       # one line at a time

summary = {"date": "2026-03-14", "guests": len(names)}
with open("summary.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(summary, f, indent=2)            # Python dict -> JSON text

with open("summary.json") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)                      # JSON text -> Python dict
print(loaded["guests"])

import json
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("data")
for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.csv")):           # every CSV export in the folder
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        print(path.name, len(f.readlines()) - 1, "rows")
# feb.csv 1 rows
# jan.csv 1 rows

(folder / "note.txt").write_text("Café Lumière", encoding="utf-8")
print((folder / "note.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))   # Café Lumière

record = {"when": datetime(2026, 3, 14, 9, 30), "total": Decimal("19.99")}
try:
    json.dumps(record)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
# TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable

print(json.dumps(record, default=str))
# {"when": "2026-03-14 09:30:00", "total": "19.99"}
safe = {"when": record["when"].isoformat(), "total": str(record["total"])}

add_glossary: Nested data
Data where dicts and lists sit inside other dicts and lists, as in most API responses.
json_normalize
A pandas function that flattens nested JSON records into a table, naming columns like customer.name.
Lambda
A small unnamed function written on one line, such as lambda r: r["amount"].
Aliasing
Two variable names pointing at the same list or dict, so changing one changes the other.
Deep copy
A copy that also copies every inner list and dict, made with copy.deepcopy.
Counter
A dict from the collections module that counts how often each value appears.
defaultdict
A dict that creates a default value, such as an empty list, for a missing key.

The standard-library module for building and looping over file paths on any operating system.

add_subtopics.title: Sorting, reshaping and stacking
add_subtopics.body:
After cleaning, most work is rearranging a table into the shape a question needs.

sort_values("amount", ascending=False) orders rows, largest first. value_counts() counts how often each value appears in a column, which is the fastest way to see categories and spot typos. nlargest(5, "amount") gives the top five rows directly. rename(columns={"amount": "revenue"}) gives columns business-friendly names.

Every DataFrame has an index, the labels on the left. groupby puts the group key into the index, so after df.groupby("region")["amount"].sum() region is no longer a normal column. reset_index() turns the index back into a column, which you need before a merge or saving a clean file, and set_index("region") does the reverse so you can look rows up by label with .loc.

Excel exports are often wide: one row per store and one column per month (Jan, Feb, Mar). That is easy to read but hard to analyse, because you cannot group by month. melt turns wide into long: one row per store and month, with a month column and a value column. Long tables are what groupby, charts and databases expect. pivot_table does the reverse when the customer wants the wide view back.

When the data comes as twelve monthly files with the same columns, pd.concat stacks them into one table. Add a column saying which file each row came from, and pass ignore_index=True so the row numbers restart cleanly.
add_subtopics.example: Tidewater Outfitters sends a budget sheet with one column per month and twelve monthly order files. The FDE melts the budget into store, month and sales columns so it can be grouped. She stacks the order files with pd.concat after tagging each with its month, then uses value_counts on region and finds "Nrth" three times, a typo to fix before any totals.

import io
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("""order_id,region,amount
1001,North,120.50
1002,South,60.00
1003,North,1250.00
1004,East,80.00
1005,North,45.00
"""))
print(orders.sort_values("amount", ascending=False)["order_id"].tolist())
# [1003, 1001, 1004, 1002, 1005]
print(orders["region"].value_counts().to_dict())    # {'North': 3, 'South': 1, 'East': 1}
print(orders.nlargest(2, "amount")["order_id"].tolist())   # [1003, 1001]

totals = orders.groupby("region")["amount"].sum()    # region is now the INDEX
print(totals.index.name)                             # region
flat = totals.reset_index().rename(columns={"amount": "revenue"})
print(flat.columns.tolist())                         # ['region', 'revenue']
print(flat.set_index("region").loc["East", "revenue"])   # 80.0

# A wide Excel-style export: one column per month
wide = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["North", "South"],
                     "Jan": [100, 80], "Feb": [120, 90], "Mar": [130, 70]})
long = wide.melt(id_vars="store", var_name="month", value_name="sales")
print(long.head(3))
#    store month  sales
# 0  North   Jan    100
# 1  South   Jan     80
# 2  North   Feb    120
print(long.groupby("store")["sales"].sum().to_dict())   # {'North': 350, 'South': 240}

# Stack monthly files that share the same columns
jan = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2], "amount": [10.0, 20.0]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [3], "amount": [15.0]})
year = pd.concat([jan.assign(month="Jan"), feb.assign(month="Feb")], ignore_index=True)
print(len(year), year["amount"].sum())               # 3 45.0

add_subtopics.title: Excel in and out for business users
add_subtopics.body:
Business users live in Excel, so many files arrive as .xlsx and many answers must go back as .xlsx. pandas reads and writes them with the openpyxl package (pip install openpyxl).

Customer workbooks are rarely clean tables. pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=None) reads every sheet at once and returns a dict of sheet name to DataFrame; sheet_name="North" reads one. Reports often start with a title row and blank rows, so skiprows=2 skips them, or header=2 says the column names are on the third row (counting from 0). Merged header cells arrive as a name followed by Unnamed: 3 columns, so rename those by hand. usecols="A:D" reads only some columns.

Dates can arrive as serial numbers such as 46083, because Excel stores a date as the number of days since 30 December 1899. Convert them with pd.to_datetime(col, unit="D", origin="1899-12-30"). Check a few dates against the file by eye.

To hand results back, write with to_excel(path, index=False) so there is no stray index column. To write several sheets into one workbook, open a pd.ExcelWriter in a with block and call to_excel once per sheet. Put a short summary on the first sheet and the detail after it. Keep money as numbers, not text, so the finance team can still sum them, and never overwrite the customer's original file.
add_subtopics.example: Tidewater's finance team sends sales_q1.xlsx with one sheet per region, a title row and a blank row on top, and dates showing as numbers like 46083. The FDE reads all sheets with sheet_name=None and skiprows=2, converts the serial dates, and returns for_finance.xlsx with a Summary sheet and an Orders sheet that they open in Excel straight away.
add_subtopics.code:
import pandas as pd   # reading and writing .xlsx needs: pip install openpyxl

# The workbook has one sheet per region. Each sheet starts with a title row
# and a blank row, so the real header is on row 3: skip the first 2 rows.
sheets = pd.read_excel("sales_q1.xlsx", sheet_name=None, skiprows=2)
print(list(sheets))                        # ['North', 'South']  (dict of DataFrames)
print(sheets["North"].columns.tolist())    # ['order_id', 'order_date', 'amount']

df = pd.concat(sheets, names=["region", "row"]).reset_index(level="region")
print(df["order_date"].tolist())           # [46083, 46087, 46085]  serial numbers!

# Excel stores dates as days since 30 December 1899
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], unit="D", origin="1899-12-30")
print(df["order_date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist())
# ['2026-03-02', '2026-03-06', '2026-03-04']

summary = df.groupby("region", as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
with pd.ExcelWriter("for_finance.xlsx") as writer:      # one file, several sheets
    summary.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Summary", index=False)
    df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Orders", index=False)
print(pd.ExcelFile("for_finance.xlsx").sheet_names)     # ['Summary', 'Orders']

add_subtopics.title: Working in Jupyter notebooks
add_subtopics.body:
A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb file) mixes code cells, their output and notes in one page that runs in the browser. It is the most common way to explore a customer's data: load a file in one cell, look at it, try a fix in the next cell, and keep the tables and charts right beside the code. VS Code opens notebooks too.

Make the notebook use your project's virtual environment. Install ipykernel in the venv and register it as a kernel, then pick that kernel in the notebook. Otherwise import pandas may load a different version, or fail.

The big trap is hidden state. Cells can run in any order, and variables stay in memory after you delete or edit the cell that made them. A notebook can look correct and still depend on a cell that no longer exists. Before you trust or share a result, use Restart Kernel and Run All: if it runs top to bottom without errors, the result is real.

Outputs are saved inside the file. A notebook that printed df.head() on customer data now contains that data, and committing it to Git leaks it. Clear outputs before committing, or install nbstripout so Git strips them automatically.

Notebooks are for exploring and explaining. When code must run every night, be tested or be reviewed, move it into a .py module (for example src/cleaning.py) and have the notebook import it, or convert the notebook to a script with nbconvert. A good rule is: once you copy a cell into a second notebook, it belongs in a module.
add_subtopics.example: An FDE exploring Tidewater's orders in a notebook gets a total of 1,450.50 and pastes it into an email. Before sending, she runs Restart Kernel and Run All, and a cell fails: it used a variable from a cell she had deleted. She fixes the order, moves the cleaning steps into src/cleaning.py, and sets up nbstripout so no customer rows are committed with the notebook.

# with uv instead:  uv run --with jupyter jupyter lab

#   %load_ext autoreload

Reused or scheduled code lives in a .py module, imported by the notebook

replace_subtopics.title: Selecting, filtering and assigning
replace_subtopics.body:
To read one column use df["amount"], which gives a Series. A list of names, df[["order_id", "amount"]], gives a smaller DataFrame. To choose rows, build a mask: a Series of True and False, one per row, such as df["region"] == "North". Putting a mask inside df[...] keeps only the True rows. Combine masks with & (and), | (or) and ~ (not), and wrap each condition in brackets, because Python's operator order would otherwise mix them up.

.loc selects by labels: df.loc[rows, columns], where rows can be a mask. .iloc selects by position number, like the first row or the third column. Use .loc when you also want to change values: df.loc[mask, "region"] = "West" updates only the matching rows. Chained indexing such as df[mask]["region"] = "West" never updates df in pandas 3 (Copy-on-Write): it only shows a ChainedAssignmentError warning. Always use df.loc[mask, "region"] = "West".

New columns are made by assigning to a new name. Keep the rule readable, for example a needs_review flag for large orders.

A few more filters cover most real requests. .isin(["North", "West"]) keeps rows whose value is in a list, much shorter than several == checks joined with |. .between(50, 150) keeps a range, including both ends. For text, .str.contains(r"INV-\d{4}", na=False) matches a regular expression (a text pattern) and treats missing values as no match; without na=False, empty cells produce NaN and the filter fails. .str.extract(r"INV-(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<num>\d{5})") pulls pieces of text into new columns, one per named group. The dataformats topic teaches the regex patterns themselves.

df.query("region == 'North' and amount > 100") writes the same filter as readable text, which is handy for long conditions.
replace_subtopics.example: Brambleton's finance lead wants every order of 1,000 or more checked by hand. The FDE adds needs_review = amount >= 1000, which flags order 1003. The sales team also says Chen Wei moved to the West region, so df.loc[df["customer"] == "Chen Wei", "region"] = "West" updates just his rows. Filtering North orders over 100 returns orders 1001 and 1003, and the North total is 1,370.50. Brambleton also wants every order whose note quotes an invoice number. str.contains with na=False finds them, and str.extract puts the invoice numbers in their own column.

import io
import pandas as pd

raw = """order_id,customer,region,amount
1001,Ana Ruiz,North,120.50
1002,Ben Okafor,South,60.00
1003,Ana Ruiz,North,1250.00
1004,Chen Wei,East,80.00
"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(raw))

print(df["customer"].tolist())             # one column is a Series
# ['Ana Ruiz', 'Ben Okafor', 'Ana Ruiz', 'Chen Wei']
print(df[["order_id", "amount"]].shape)    # a list of columns is a DataFrame: (4, 2)
print(df.iloc[0]["customer"])              # iloc: by position -> Ana Ruiz
print(df.loc[df["region"] == "North", "amount"].sum())   # loc: mask + column -> 1370.5

big_north = df[(df["region"] == "North") & (df["amount"] > 100)]   # & needs brackets
print(big_north["order_id"].tolist())      # [1001, 1003]

df["needs_review"] = df["amount"] >= 1000          # new column from a rule
df.loc[df["customer"] == "Chen Wei", "region"] = "West"   # fix matching rows only
print(df[["order_id", "region", "needs_review"]])
#    order_id region  needs_review
# 0      1001  North         False
# 1      1002  South         False
# 2      1003  North          True
# 3      1004   West         False

# More filters
notes = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003, 1004],
    "region": ["North", "South", "North", "West"],
    "amount": [120.5, 60.0, 1250.0, 80.0],
    "note": ["ref INV-2026-00042", None, "urgent, ref INV-2026-00077", "call back"],
})
print(notes[notes["region"].isin(["North", "West"])]["order_id"].tolist())  # [1001, 1003, 1004]
print(notes[notes["amount"].between(50, 150)]["order_id"].tolist())        # [1001, 1002, 1004]
has_inv = notes["note"].str.contains(r"INV-\d{4}", na=False)   # na=False: None counts as no match
print(has_inv.tolist())                                        # [True, False, True, False]
print(notes["note"].str.extract(r"INV-(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<num>\d{5})")["num"].tolist())
# ['00042', nan, '00077', nan]
print(notes.query("region == 'North' and amount > 100")["order_id"].tolist())   # [1001, 1003]

notes[notes["region"] == "West"]["region"] = "East"   # chained: pandas 3 warns
# ChainedAssignmentError: A value is being set on a copy of a DataFrame ...
print(notes["region"].tolist())            # ['North', 'South', 'North', 'West']  unchanged!
notes.loc[notes["region"] == "West", "region"] = "East"      # the right way
print(notes["region"].tolist())            # ['North', 'South', 'North', 'East']

replace_subtopics.title: Missing data, dtypes and dates
replace_subtopics.body:
Missing values show as NaN (not a number) for numbers and NaT (not a time) for dates. df.isna() marks them. You have three honest options: leave them and report them, drop the rows with dropna, or fill them with fillna. Filling a missing amount with 0 changes totals and averages, so only do it when the customer agrees that blank really means zero. A safe habit is to add a flag column first, so the gap stays visible.

Fix dtypes on purpose. Tidy text with .str methods such as str.strip() (remove spaces) and str.title(). Turn text into numbers with pd.to_numeric; errors="coerce" turns anything unreadable into NaN instead of crashing, so count the NaN values afterwards to see what failed.

Dates need an explicit format. 03/04/2026 is 4 March in the US and 3 April in the UK, and pandas cannot know which one the customer meant. Ask, then parse with format="%m/%d/%Y" or "%d/%m/%Y". If a column mixes formats, parse each format separately with errors="coerce" and combine the results. Once a column is a datetime, .dt gives parts such as month and day name.

Big files need a few extra habits. usecols=[...] reads only the columns you need. dtype={"order_id": "int32"} sets smaller types up front. The category dtype stores a column with few distinct values, such as region, as small codes plus one list of labels, often using a fraction of the memory. For a file larger than RAM, chunksize=100_000 returns the file in pieces you process one at a time, for example adding up totals.

Once a big file is clean, save it as Parquet with to_parquet (needs pyarrow). Parquet is compressed, reads much faster than CSV, and keeps dtypes, so dates and categories come back correct without re-parsing. The dataformats topic compares Parquet and CSV.
replace_subtopics.example: Brambleton confirms their store system writes US dates. The FDE strips spaces from " North ", title-cases "south", removes commas and converts amount to float64, then flags the one missing amount instead of filling it. Dates are parsed twice (ISO format and US format) and combined. The row that says "not recorded" stays NaT, and the FDE asks the store manager whether that order date can be recovered. Later Brambleton sends a 5 GB export with 60 columns. Reading three columns with usecols, a category region and smaller number types makes the table fit in memory, and the FDE saves the clean result as Parquet for the next run.
replace_subtopics.code:
import io
import pandas as pd

raw = """order_id,customer,order_date,region,amount
1001,Ana Ruiz,2026-03-02,North,120.50
1002,Ben Okafor,03/04/2026,south,
1003,Ana Ruiz,2026-03-05, North ,"1,250.00"
1005,Dara Singh,not recorded,North,45.00
"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(raw))

print(df.isna().sum()["amount"])                     # 1 missing amount
df["region"] = df["region"].str.strip().str.title()  # " North " and "south" -> tidy
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["amount_missing"] = df["amount"].isna()           # flag it; do not guess a value

# Two date formats in one column: parse each, then combine
iso = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
us = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], format="%m/%d/%Y", errors="coerce")
df["order_date"] = iso.fillna(us)                    # "not recorded" stays NaT

print(df.dtypes["amount"], df.dtypes["order_date"])  # float64 datetime64[us] (pandas 2: [ns])
print(df[["region", "amount", "amount_missing", "order_date"]])
#   region  amount  amount_missing order_date
# 0  North   120.5           False 2026-03-02
# 1  South     NaN            True 2026-03-04
# 2  North  1250.0           False 2026-03-05
# 3  North    45.0           False        NaT
print(df["order_date"].dt.day_name().tolist())      # .dt gives date parts
# ['Monday', 'Wednesday', 'Thursday', nan]


# ---- Big files ----
# Pretend this is a 5 GB export with many columns; we need only three of them
csv_text = "order_id,region,amount,notes\n" + "".join(
    f"{i},{['North', 'South', 'East'][i % 3]},{i % 50}.5,long free text here\n" for i in range(9000))

full = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text))
print(full.memory_usage(deep=True).sum())      # 501132 bytes: every column, default types

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text), usecols=["order_id", "region", "amount"],
                 dtype={"order_id": "int32", "amount": "float32"})
df["region"] = df["region"].astype("category")   # 3 repeated labels -> category
print(df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum())        # 81171 bytes: about 6 times smaller

# chunksize reads the file in pieces, so it never has to fit in RAM at once
total = 0.0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text), usecols=["amount"], chunksize=2000):
    total += chunk["amount"].sum()
print(round(total, 1))                          # 225000.0

df.to_parquet("orders.parquet")                 # needs: pip install pyarrow
back = pd.read_parquet("orders.parquet")
print(back["order_id"].dtype, back["region"].dtype, back["amount"].dtype)
# int32 category float32   <- types survive, unlike a CSV

replace_subtopics.title: groupby, aggregation and pivot tables
replace_subtopics.body:
Most customer questions are summaries: revenue by region, orders per month, average basket by channel. groupby does this in three steps, often called split, apply, combine. It splits rows into groups by a column, applies a calculation such as sum or mean to each group, and combines the results into a new table with one row per group.

Named aggregation, as in .agg(revenue=("amount", "sum")), lets you compute several summaries at once and choose clear column names. A pivot table (pivot_table) spreads one grouping down the side and another across the top, which is what business users know from Excel.

Two details matter. sum and mean skip NaN values silently, so a group whose amounts are all missing shows 0.0 revenue, which looks like a real zero. And to group by month, convert a datetime with .dt.to_period("M") so 2 March and 29 March land in the same group.

Sometimes you need the group result on every row instead of one row per group. transform does that: df.groupby("region")["revenue"].transform("sum") returns the region total next to each store, so revenue / region_total gives each store's share of its region.

Week-over-week questions use a few time tools. resample("W") groups a table indexed by dates into weeks ("M" or "ME" months, "D" days). shift(1) moves values down one row, so each week sits next to last week's value. pct_change() gives the percentage change from the previous row. cumsum() gives a running total. rolling(7).mean() gives a moving average over the last 7 rows, which smooths out daily noise.
replace_subtopics.example: Brambleton's operations director asks: which region brings the most revenue, and is web growing against stores? groupby on region shows North with 3 orders and 1,415.50 in revenue, but an average order of 471.83 driven by one large order. The pivot shows web at 120.50 in March and 1,250.00 in April. The FDE points out that April web is one order, so it is too early to call a trend. Brambleton's director then asks for each store's share of its region and weekly revenue with the change from last week. transform gives the shares, and resample("W") with pct_change shows growth slowing from 30.4 to 18.9 percent.
